groups.title: Password hashing and JWT security internals
groups.question: Your PERN app stores user passwords and gives logged-in users a JWT. Explain how passwords should be stored so a stolen database doesn't reveal them, and what a JWT contains and protects.

followUps.bcrypt's adaptive work factor and per-pa: Why does bcrypt use a salt and a cost factor, and why not just hash the password with SHA-256?
followUps.JWT structure: header.payload.signature: Anyone can decode a JWT's payload. So what does the signature protect, and what must never go in the payload?

evidence.text: bcrypt adds a random salt per password, so identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables don't work.
Its cost factor makes each hash deliberately slow, so guessing passwords at scale is very expensive, and it can be raised as hardware gets faster.
At login the entered password is hashed and compared; the original password is never stored or decrypted.

notEnough: Only saying hash passwords with bcrypt without explaining the salt or the slowness.

misconceptions.text: Says passwords should be encrypted so they can be decrypted later.

evidence.text: A JWT has a header, a payload of claims and a signature, each base64url-encoded.
The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it; passwords and secrets never go there.
The signature, made with the server's secret, lets the server detect any change to the header or the payload.

notEnough: Only saying a JWT has three parts without saying what the signature does.

misconceptions.text: Says the JWT payload is encrypted and safe for sensitive data.

groups.title: Web security: XSS, CSRF, and secure cookies
groups.question: Your app needs to store the auth token in the browser, and a comment field might let an attacker inject a script into other users' pages. Explain where you'd keep the token so that script can't steal it, and how you'd make sure only valid data reaches your API.

followUps.HTTP-only cookies prevent XSS from steal: How does an HTTP-only cookie stop an injected script from taking the token, and what do Secure and SameSite add?
followUps.Zod schema validation: parsing untrusted: Why validate with a schema on the server even if the React form already checks the input?

evidence.text: JavaScript can't read an HTTP-only cookie, so an injected script can't steal a token kept there, unlike one in localStorage.
Secure sends the cookie only over HTTPS, and SameSite limits sending it on cross-site requests, which helps against CSRF.

notEnough: Only saying use HTTP-only cookies without explaining what they block.

misconceptions.text: Says HTTP-only cookies stop XSS attacks from happening at all.

evidence.text: All input from outside is untrusted, so it is parsed against a schema on the server before it is used.
Invalid input is rejected with a clear error, and valid input comes out with the expected shape and types.
The same schema can be shared by the frontend and the backend, so the rules live in one place.

notEnough: Only saying validate with Zod without explaining why on the server.

groups.title: Implementing JWT auth in a PERN Express API
groups.question: Users log in to your Express API and then call protected endpoints like creating a post. Explain how the server issues tokens at login, how long they last, and how each protected request is checked.

followUps.Signing JWTs with jsonwebtoken and setti: Why keep the access token short-lived, and how does a refresh token keep the user logged in?
followUps.Auth middleware: verify Bearer token and: Walk through what the auth middleware does with the Authorization header, and what happens if the token has expired.

evidence.text: At login the server signs a token with a secret, containing claims like the user id and role, plus an expiry.
A short expiry limits how long a stolen access token can be used.
A longer-lived refresh token, kept in an HTTP-only cookie, is used to get new access tokens.

notEnough: Only saying sign a token with jsonwebtoken without explaining expiry or refresh.

evidence.text: The middleware reads the Bearer token from the Authorization header.
It verifies the signature and the expiry with the secret, and rejects the request with 401 if that fails.
On success it attaches the decoded user to req, so the handlers know who is calling.

notEnough: Only saying check the token in a middleware without the steps.

misconceptions.text: Says decoding the token is enough without verifying its signature.

groups.title: Security hardening with Zod, Helmet, and rate limiting
groups.question: Before launching your PERN app, you want to harden the API against common browser attacks, and against attackers guessing passwords on the login endpoint. Explain what you'd add and why.

followUps.helmet middleware for secure HTTP respon: What do the headers that helmet sets protect against, for example X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy?
followUps.express-rate-limit to prevent brute-forc: Why put a strict rate limit on /login specifically, and what should the client get when it's exceeded?

evidence.text: helmet sets security-related HTTP response headers on every response.
They tell the browser to block things like showing your page in a frame (clickjacking), guessing content types, or running scripts from untrusted sources.

notEnough: Only saying use helmet for security without saying what the headers do.

evidence.text: Rate limiting caps how many requests one client can make in a time window.
On login and register, it stops attackers from trying many passwords quickly.
Over the limit, the server answers 429 Too Many Requests, ideally saying when to retry.

notEnough: Only saying add rate limiting without explaining what it stops.
